<reason>Both sides were disciplined and closed-book honest, with no fake sourcing on either side. A built the cleaner decisive frame: a headline is a steering wheel, so the choice is what governments are held to, and it converted CON's own opening line ("well-being is the purpose of government") into a means-end inversion charge that CON never fully escaped. A's best move was reframing CON's housing hypothetical: GDP does not avoid weighting, it assigns silent zeros to insecurity, unpaid care and depleted nature — "unexamined weights, which is worse." That reframe survived the exchange, and A's mechanism claim ("ministers follow the headline; the dashboard does not drive Treasury cases, press coverage, or ministerial credit-taking") was only weakly answered by B's "a headline is not a monopoly over public reasoning." B did real damage in two places: it forced A to specify a headline via pressure questions, then exposed that mean life satisfaction and the low-well-being share can diverge, restoring the discretion problem A claimed to have escaped; and it correctly noted that future beneficiaries cannot self-report, so forecasting discretion returns. But A's answer — that surfacing that distributional divergence is precisely the argument democracies should have, while GDP never poses it — is a genuine response rather than an evasion, and B's alternative (separately reported outcomes plus binding standards) had already been conceded by A as compatible, which blunted its comparative force. B also drifted into repetition of "limited and legible benchmark" without deepening the growth-expands-capacity strand it opened with, and its pressure-question answer that a growth-raising policy loses whenever a standard binds left "primary" looking thinner than its case needed. A's rebuttal being clipped is a small execution cost, but the argument was already complete by then.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Two exchanges mattered most. A's turn of CON's housing example — showing GDP answers the same trade-off silently by assigning weight zero — neutralized B's central "politically elastic weights" objection. B's sharpest counter was exposing that A's newly specified mean-plus-floor headline can move in opposite directions, so respondents cannot settle how government weights different people; A partly absorbed this by arguing the divergence is a feature (visible political argument) rather than a bug, which held the line but did not fully erase the hit.</best_rebuttal>
